messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Taufa is a 42-year-old Tongan-Australian electrician living in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest, currently in a long-term relationship. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his general practitioner, whom he had visited ostensibly for sleep difficulties. His PCL-5 score of 78 places him in a range consistent with severe posttraumatic stress, and the clinical picture that has emerged across the intake and first two sessions is one of a man whose life has contracted quietly and systematically around a single night approximately fourteen months ago.

Rangi was working late on a commercial rewiring job — it was around 9 in the evening — when he was assaulted by two men in the car park of the building he had been contracted to service. The attack was sudden and prolonged. He had heard the car park door slam behind him as he carried equipment to his van, and within seconds he was struck from behind. What followed involved repeated blows and, at one point, one of the men grabbing him by the collar and forcing his face against the side of the vehicle. He does not have a continuous memory of the assault. What he retains are discrete images: the grain of the van's panelling close to his eyes, the specific quality of the light from a single overhead lamp, the sensation of cold asphalt under his hands. He describes these not as memories so much as photographs he did not choose to keep, each one sharp and bounded, with nothing connecting them. The gaps between those images disturb him almost as much as the images themselves. He has come to believe that what happened in those missing intervals must have been worse than what he can recall, and that not knowing is itself a kind of evidence of something he cannot face.

He returned to work within two weeks, which he now recognises as a mistake — not because he was unfit, he insists, but because he is certain the assault happened to him for reasons rooted in who he is. He has said, with quiet conviction, that another man, a more careful or more capable man, would not have been alone in that car park at that hour, would have noticed something, would have walked differently. This belief has settled into him like a structural fault: invisible from the outside, load-bearing. When he recalls the attack, the guilt that surfaces is immediate and physical, a tightening across his chest that he finds difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss.

The evenings have become the hardest part of his day. As 9 p.m. approaches, something shifts in him that he cannot always name in advance — a loosening of the boundary between then and now, a feeling that the world is becoming slightly less real, that he is watching himself from somewhere nearby. On job sites, which often require him to move through unfamiliar commercial buildings, he finds himself mapping exits and sightlines before he can begin work. When a colleague moves suddenly into his peripheral vision, or lays a hand on his shoulder to get his attention, his body responds before his mind catches up — a lurch, a raised arm, a surge of adrenaline that takes long minutes to subside. Doors are particularly difficult. The sound of a heavy door slamming — a common enough event on construction sites — can stop him mid-task.

Over the months since the assault, Rangi has quietly reorganised his evenings around his phone and a games console, staying absorbed in screens until he is too tired to lie awake. He drinks most nights, usually alone after his partner has gone to bed, and he has stopped watching anything on television that might touch the subject of violence or assault. His partner has noticed the drinking and the withdrawal, and the distance between them has grown in ways neither has directly named. He has declined two social invitations from workmates in the past three months, citing tiredness.

What finally brought him to his GP was a comment his partner made — gently, he says, not as a criticism — that she no longer recognised the person he was becoming. What frightens him most, sitting in the consulting room, is the possibility that she is right, and that there is no version of himself left to recover. What he hopes for, more tentatively, is that he might be wrong about that.
